questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Personal connection to the destination (heritage / friends there/ etc.)

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: My decision to go on exchange in Berlin was motivated by a number of things, and primary among them was the desire to deepen my understanding and connection to Germany through language and immersion. I had considered other smaller german cities, yet Berlin won out considering the size, number of possibilities, university offerings, cultural experiences and geographical location. In addition to this, I had always dreamed of coming to the city to stay, and even though it was enticing to visit a smaller and less known destination, the idea of actually *living* in Berlin seemed to offer something other than any mere visit could, so despite having been here many times, I chose to deepen my relation to it by going on exchange here.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I would probably recommend students going on exchange to think carefully and pay attention to what they actually feel their expectations and priorities are - are they based on abstract ideas of spatial belonging, academic aspirations, cultural curiosity, or something completely other? I feel that the destination of your student exchange will always be unable to live up every single thing that you have thought beforehand, yet I think you can get much closer to having a fantastic experience if you're honest with yourself about what you want, and maybe less strict about where (friends, family, societal-) expectations would want you to go.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: I found that the information was well delegated. I received a lot of emails from the school detailing practical information regarding both my citizenship status in Berlin, what regulations I needed to comply with at the school and in the public system of Germany, as well as general information regarding my stay. In addition, a lot of online resources were available for exchange students at services such as 'distributedcampus' and the homepages of Freie University.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I received assistance in a number of ways. Before arriving, I contacted a student that had been in Berlin before, and questioned them on school procedures and it really helped a lot. Secondly, I attended the orientation days at the school in the second week of October, which (although very short) gave a good introduction to how to apply to courses and stuff life that at the school. Thirdly, I have used the information services at the school, both the Erasmus+ office at the central bureau, and the one specific to my institute, and they have always been available and helpful to answer any questions I had.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
It was not easy to find off campus housing, and I was very lucky to find it through a personal contact through my family. I would recommend anyone going to Berlin to check out
wg-gesucht.de
or
immobilienscout24.de
regularly, and actively write to landlords through these services. In addition, check out ex-patriot groups from your country of origin on Facebook - they often have helpful information and rental opportunities. If you do not find anything before coming here, and are living temporarily in a hostel or something like that, go to school and check out the messaging boards + ask around for advice - sometimes rooms get posted here and more often than not people are very willing to give advice on where to look for rooms. You can also post a small introduction to yourself and what you are seeking here!

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
It is a huge city, and you can honestly expect to spend at least 45 minutes of transport no matter where you end up living. But living off campus is also very fun, and you get to have the feel of independence in Berlin, which is really nice. There are a number of administrative measures you will have to go through, such as making an "Anmeldung" at your local municipal bureau, but these are easily googlable. 

I would recommend living off-campus - Berlin has so many great neighbourhoods, and people are really attached to their local "Kiez" as they are called. Take time to notice the distinct vibe in your area, the gathering-spots and their frequents and the specific popular attractions of your Kiez - everyone has something really great.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I did not make use of student housing, but from what I could garner, I thought it seemed rather limited and pricey. There are too few of the Wohngemeinschaft rooms available for students, and the privately contracted places just seem horrendous.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: You need to attend the orientation days and watch the videos at 'distributed campus' in order to understand the procedure for course registration - trust me! It can be a little confusing and hard, as there are specific rules for each institute on where, what level and how many courses you are allowed to take across FU and other universities as well. But it is ultimately manageable if you go to orientation days and ask Erasmus+ coordinators if you need help.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
You have to find the courses in the online Course Catalog, and then register through a website called 'Campus Management'. When finding your courses on CM, you can use a step-by-step video made available on the 'distributed campus' website (just search course registration). There is a really long course registration period where you can shop around and sign up for many courses - just remember to sign off before the period ends. Also be really aware of what the requirements for obtaining credits are, and how the courses tie together with your schedule.  

If you want to take courses outside of your institute you cannot sign up through CM and will have to go to the first lectures and ask the professor if you can take part in the course (alternatively, shoot them an email). This has implications for how you will obtain your grades at the end of the semester, seeing as grades are issued through CM - you will have to get the information form the Erasmus+ office.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: I was helped by the Erasmus+ office on several occasions, as well as speaking to other Erasmus students. Additionally, 'distributed campus' was helpful. Do not hesitate to make use of these resources.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all the courses I wanted - two of them were in another institute than my own, and it was ultimately quite easy to figure out. The professors are quite flexible with regards to requirements and are often very helpful if you have questions. I did not expect to get all the courses that I wanted, but even though some of the classes were "full", I was allowed to participate.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Ask what professors are inspiring before hand and try something outside of your academic comfort zone if you have electives. Attend the orientation days and use 'distributed campus'. 

Do not worry too much about getting the literature lists before hand if you need to get courses pre-approved at your home uni. - many of the professors are really bad at answering their e-mails, and they often do not finalize the course readings before the start of the semester. I spent a lot of time trying to track down course readings to apply for pre-approval of my courses at my home institution, and it ended up being a very energy demanding and draining experience. I would just wait till your courses have started to gather them up and apply.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I thought the level was below my home-university in most courses. It was ultimately a matter of class structure and organization. Many of the courses require student inputs as part of the requirements for obtaining credits, and these often led to somewhat disenchanting classroom experiences with discussions that were not adequately structured and awkward silences. On the other hand, there is a lot of direct contact with professors - do try to make use of their availability! Ask questions, be curious and try to engage with the class discussions.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: Both

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I did not feel any difference between the masters and the bachelor courses in terms of difficulty. I had 4 obligatory bachelor courses and two masters courses on another institute, and it worked really well. The biggest difference between courses is the amount of work required to obtain credits, but that has nothing to do with the level, only the professors requirements.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: As mentioned before, it was much less structured, with almost no lectures and ultimately mostly class based discussions of readings. Therefore, it was a big difference to UCPH, where we often have lectures with accompanying tuition sessions by student instructors. Here there almost only seems to be 1 session a week, and it seems exclusively to be class sessions with a professor, which are often dominated by student inputs. It varies slightly from class to class how this looks and how much the professor structures the debate. On the other hand, it brings out a lot of student perspectives that are interesting, but I find the style of teaching at UCPH better suited to my learning style.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Global Political Economy
Critical Political Ecology: Between Marxism and Environmentalism 
Thinking Sex: Radical Theories of the Politics of Sexuality 
Political Polarization in the US
Democratic Institutions and Development with a special focus on Africa
Politics of European Integration

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would recommend Critical Political Ecology: Between Marxism and Environmentalism by Markus Kienscherf and Political Polarization in the US with Christian Lammert. These were taught at a high level and had professors that were extremely engaging.

questions.question: Insurance DKK *
Housing DKK per month *
Books DKK per month *
Local transportation DKK per month *
Food DKK per month *
Personal spending DKK per month *
Communication (phone, internet, etc.) DKK per month *
Other fees DKK per month *
What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer:
You have to pay a fee for using the german TV and radio if you register your adress in Berlin. This amounts to about 18 eur. a month. 
You also have to pay a mandatory semester fee which amounts to about 286 eur. This covers your use of public transport through the whole of Berlin for the whole semester however! But it is mandatory. It can be extended to the whole of Germany for an extra fee - I would recommend checking this out if you plan on travelling inside Germany.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Food and drinks are much less expensive than in Denmark, especially for restaurants and bars.
Housing is more or less the same. 
Vintage clothes and second-hand stores are more expensive than expected.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I found it a little hard to connect with non-academic opportunities, but there are a lot of offerings. They are exhibited at the start of the semester in the orientation days. Sign up very early for Erasmus+ specific events, as they have very limited space - I was only able to get space for 1 out of 10.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
There are very good sports opportunities and they are also very cheap. Sign up for courses during the orientation days! Everything from dancing, curling, karate to bouldering and mountaineering are available. 
The student cafees at the different institutes have a lot of events - very often in german, but whispering translations are often offered  - that can be really nice to try! There are some centrally organized parties as well, but to be honest they were only attended by Erasmus+ students.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I took a university sports course in bouldering which was really cool. Do try to book in advance as the slots are quickly filled. 
In addition, as mentioned before, check out your local institutes student cafe and keep an eye out for events. The North American JFK Institute especially has a lot of english events offered regularly.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
I recommend trying out the Berlin nightlife, including music venues, clubs, and public events, as well as going to restaurants, bars, and cafes. Try to romanticize your experience and catch the pulse of the city. Berlin really has something for everyone. As mentioned before, dive into your local neighbourhoods' hidden gems and its history. 
Also try to get out of Berlin and visit Potsdam or some of the surrounding lakes and cities. There is a lot of beautiful nature and lovely experiences.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy - there are a lot of commonalities between Copenhagen and Berlin.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: People often have a lot of different courses, and do not necessarily have a group that they follow, so they are maybe more open to talking to strangers than you would expect of UCPH! Try to strike up a conversation, and do it early on - people are very open. Attend events of your interests at the school as well, and I'm sure you will find friends. If you are more to the introverted side, using the sports offerings or specific events at school can help give a frame of common interest.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: I did not find any cultural differences particularly challenging. People are a bit more overtly political in their attitudes and behaviors here, which I think is refreshing. There are a lot of demonstrations and protests at the Uni. and in Berlin in general - I had good experiences talking to people and attending these, but it was not a challenge.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I appreciated the pluralism of Berlin a lot - as mentioned before, people are more political, and I also found that they also "inhabit" their preferences in a thorough and authentic way because there are so many sub-cultures and communities for almost every single identity or interest. This provides a very heterogenous public, and it is clearly visible in the school and the city at large.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1) Think carefully about the amount of courses you choose, their credit distribution, and the workload of each course - there are many possiblities, and it can become relatively less or more overwhelming to complete the 30 ECTS requirement depending on how you mix and match. Also, try to take a course outside of your institute. 
2) The FU is a relatively open and smooth functioning university, so make good use of the campus. There are many libraries, study halls and (really well priced) cafeterias to visit. 
3) Talk to people early on, and do not be afraid to feel at home in using the student cafes or other places. The earlier you try this, the more time you will have to hang out with your new friends.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
A random list: 
1) Try to ask fellow students which courses and professors they recommend.
2) You have a number of student benefits, including a 6-month free Amazon Prime subscription, and other discounts as a FU student. 
3) Use the Mensa's (cantine's/cafeterias) - especially the Asian one called Mensa II has sushi and is really nice and cheap.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The most rewarding part was the experince of living in Berlin. I did like the school and most of the courses I took did enlighten me, yet I must say the best thing was simply having each weekend in Berlin. There are so many good things to do and places to see! It was also very wholesome to meet new people here, and I found a number of really good friends through the school and Erasmus+.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The greatest challenge is managing your time between immersing yourself and slowing down to take time to notice, whilst also having to comply with school requirements and bureaucratic hurdles (especially UCPH requirements such as pre-approvals), all the time trying to get as much out of your experience as possible. I would say a trick to managing this is recognizing that you have limits and taking time to identify when to take breaks and when to push yourself a bit.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
